When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible. It did not make training better.

TL;DR: An exact oracle scores explanations of an authorization policy against ground truth. A 4B student taught by the algorithm reaches 92% on its own policy, learns a fixed schedule of checks that does not transfer, and RL only changes the strategy.

Hyperbolic representations are well suited to taxonomies because they accommodate hierarchical growth, yet a single global interpretation of distance and radial depth can be restrictive when local geometric contexts vary across concepts. We introduce TaxoScale, a taxonomy representation framework centered on concept-conditioned geometric scaling in one shared Poincaré space. A shared predictor maps each concept's coordinate, radial depth, and training-visible neighbor-distance statistics to a positive scale, which recalibrates task-facing radial depth and pairwise dissimilarity without moving the underlying coordinates. Across ten taxonomies, a unified three-seed benchmark compares TaxoScale with thirteen external baseline configurations spanning order, hyperbolic, box-based ontology, and recent hierarchy encoders. TaxoScale attains the highest aggregate mean F1 in all four reported regimes; paired taxonomy-level bootstrap intervals support positive average differences over official-code HiT in the two hard-negative regimes, while the random-negative intervals cross zero. Matched controls show that local scaling improves over no scaling and a learned global scale, persists after independent margin retuning, and benefits from jointly calibrating radial depth and pairwise dissimilarity. Candidate-pool stress tests on WordNetNoun and DOID.diseases further show that the ranking gap over HiT grows as the pool expands from 11 to 1001 candidates. Curvature, coarse-scale, unseen-anchor, residual-scorer, input, lookup, fusion, ranking, hierarchy, and efficiency diagnostics characterize both the mechanism and its boundaries.

TL;DR: TaxoScale learns concept-conditioned scalar calibrations of hyperbolic depth and distance, improving hard-negative taxonomy prediction while retaining one shared Poincaré representation.

Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. In mathematics and code the verifier is exact. Outside them it is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be distinguished from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level. Executable authorization policies over an enumerable space of 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. That turns the causal fidelity of a model's cited reasons into a computed quantity. We compile such policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear, each with its own behavioural signature. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding. The sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on n = 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching. Noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. Before any training, a model-free audit of the verifier alone predicts which phenotype a run will produce. It measures the verifier's selection error and the sign of its gap, and a short pilot adds how often the reward saturates. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the audit quantity is invariant and the phenotypes recur. Sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps stay the steeper branch on the replication grid too, 3.2× against 2.3×, on an interval too wide to test the size of the asymmetry. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and a second task family of 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles, on which the audit reads the same way.

TL;DR: We build a setting where the true process reward is exactly computable, degrade the verifier seven ways, and show that a model-free audit of the verifier alone predicts which of four reward-hacking phenotypes training will produce.

Forecasting a newly listed item before it has any observations means predicting from its metadata alone. In this strict cold-start regime ($L=0$), what the metadata has to supply splits in two. Trajectory shape transfers from semantically retrieved neighbours. Scale does not, and has to be regressed from the target's own embedding. We test that split by corrupting the retrieval graph, and the two error terms move apart. Damaging neighbour metadata moves shape error by 3.1 to 13.1% across nine datasets while leaving scale error inside 0.9%, and under total retrieval failure accuracy degrades to the retrieval-free prior rather than past it. The decomposition is not specific to our model. Supplying the same aggregated-neighbour features to a gradient-boosted tree improves it on all nine datasets, by 1.41 to 3.70%. We instantiate the decomposition as RAID (Retrieval-Augmented Iterative Diffusion), which adds a gated diffusion head over the retrieval prior, and find the head buys calibration rather than point accuracy, closing 56% of the prior's gap to the nominal 80% interval while leaving sMAPE close to level. Against the retrieval-augmented tree RAID wins four datasets, ties three and loses two on sMAPE, and transfers zero-shot across Latin, Cyrillic and Hanzi scripts without retraining, which a per-dataset tree cannot do. Against Chronos it is 37x faster end to end. Which datasets RAID wins remains open. Metadata richness predicts the margin in the expected direction but does not reach significance at nine datasets.

TL;DR: At zero history, trajectory shape transfers from metadata-retrieved neighbours and scale does not; the two fail independently, and the decomposition helps a gradient-boosted tree as much as it helps our model.

Portable Executable malware has remained a persistent and growing threat to digital infrastructures, making malware family classification an active research area. In recent years, deep learning models have achieved promising results, yet their accuracy drops sharply under concept drift, and they are often black boxes, providing no explanation for their predictions. In this paper, we propose MalReX, a robust and explainable framework that addresses both gaps with a unified design. MalReX builds a Canonical Executable Graph for each malware binary from its code blocks, and pools it into several decorrelated components. Beyond the cross-entropy loss, a Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion loss reduces the spurious correlations between components that break under concept drift, and a variance loss keeps every component from collapsing to a constant. For explainability, MalReX traces each prediction back to its attributed blocks using Integrated Gradients, and a frozen Large Language Model then turns them into an evidence-based report. Experiments on MalwareBazaar and MalwareDrift show that MalReX outperforms eight baselines, both in distribution and under concept drift, with the smallest drop across the drift boundary. Removing the blocks IG ranks highest drops the F1-score 29 to 37 points more than removing random ones, showing that the explanations reflect the evidence the classifier uses.

TL;DR: MalReX classifies PE malware from a graph of its code blocks, remains robust under concept drift through decorrelated components, and explains each prediction with a report grounded in the blocks the classifier relied on.

Post-training chains optimizations whose rewards each name only some of the behaviors a deployed model must keep. We follow one 30B-parameter, 3B-active mixture-of-experts policy, serving English and eight Indic languages, through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR), reinforcement learning against a generative reward model we train (RLHF), and on-policy distillation (OPD), scoring every checkpoint on the same 35 benchmarks. Our 26B-total, 4B-active judge outscores a 235B-parameter generative reward model on RM-Bench, yet RLHF against it cuts extractive F1 by 24 to 38 points while improving code and knowledge: the gold span survives, wrapped in a sentence. We organize these movements with one quantity, the within-group covariance between a behavior and the advantage (the selection term of the Price equation), whose sign says whether a reward promotes, ignores, or opposes that behavior. Its corollaries say that group-relative selection cannot restore a behavior absent from sampled groups, and moves a rare one only in proportion to its mass. We watch a length bonus drive reasoning to zero as the variation that selection needs disappears, and the same mechanism explains why mixing verifiable rewards back in fails, realizing a specified 70:30 mix as 80:20 at 2.3 times the cost. OPD supplies an external target without optimizing any reward: from prompts containing no extraction, it recovers on average 81\% of each loss RLHF caused while keeping on average 67\% of each gain. Weight-space merging obeys the same account, with the rate at which a completion's log-probability grows along the weight direction as the fitness, and there it decomposes measured scores exactly. A merge along the RLHF direction trades each loss against each gain one-for-one up to a curvature term; its midpoint undoes only 49\% of the losses, and extrapolation collapses instruction following that RLHF left unchanged.

TL;DR: Post-training rewards damage behaviors they don't price. A within-group covariance predicts which drift and why RL can't restore what it stops sampling; on-policy distillation recovers 81% of RLHF's losses on average, keeping 67% of its gains.

Diffusion models can reproduce individual training images. Recent work reduces this copying by omitting an intermediate range of noise levels during training, while preserving image quality. Yet the model must still denoise at those levels during generation. In this paper, we propose a probability model that distinguishes learning patterns shared across images from reproducing individual examples. We prove that training on lightly corrupted images can improve denoising at untrained noise levels while copying stays low. The model learns shared structure with little change in the probabilities of generating individual examples. We then use the same model family to explain why copies formed midway through sampling can survive even when a low-copy model performs the final steps. Our bounds identify when those steps cannot move a sample far enough from a training image to prevent a copy, and when switching later increases copying. CIFAR-10 automobile experiments show denoising improvement across an untrained noise band. Separate controlled training comparisons show that models can learn from individual examples while rarely generating copies of them. Sampling experiments support the predicted timing effect and show that a final denoiser can preserve copies of images it was never trained on.

TL;DR: A probability model explains cross-noise learning with low copying and quantifies when copies persist after a denoiser switch.

A generative recommender must choose semantic-ID prefixes before a scorer can rank complete items. Once a useful branch is pruned, a better final ranking cannot recover it. We introduce MapRec, which brings two complementary sources of evidence to this prefix decision. A behavior-informed item index supplies the code structure, and a source-conditioned generator rereads individual interactions as its decoder state changes. MapRec then projects a fixed item scorer's preferences onto legal code branches and learns a confidence-aware residual correction around the source-refined prediction. The correction acts before trie search, while the same scorer orders the resulting item pool. On three full-catalog domains, the complete pipeline performs strongly against the displayed baselines. Ablations support the value of rank-to-prefix evidence; comparisons with simpler corrections delimit the additional benefit of iterative feedback. These results identify the interface between item-level ranking and prefix generation as the central design choice.

Early battery cycle-life prediction aims to estimate a cell's final cycle life from only a small number of early charge cycles. Existing approaches are commonly developed for fixed early-cycle windows and evaluated within individual datasets or battery chemistries, limiting their applicability to heterogeneous battery populations and variable amounts of early-cycle data. We introduce PORTAL, a physical-prototype retrieval model for cycle-life prediction from variable-length early-cycle prefixes of voltage-current charge curves. PORTAL encodes each cycle using curve patches and a physical token derived from battery descriptors, including cathode, anode, temperature, cell format, and nominal capacity. A cycle-level Transformer encodes individual charge cycles, while a masked inter-cycle MLP aggregates the observed prefix. The model further retrieves learned feature prototypes from training batteries and applies a gated residual correction, without retrieving training-set lifetime labels.
We evaluate PORTAL over all prefix lengths from 1 to 50 cycles across five battery chemistry groups derived from Tongji, CALCE, and HUST, with each experiment repeated over 10 random seeds. In the all-chemistry mixed setting with 34 test cells, PORTAL achieves a prefix-averaged MAPE of 16.01%, compared with 31.34% for Informer and 48.05% for TimesNet. Notably, even when relying strictly on the first 10 cycles as input, the MAPE result of the trained model is already similar to using all 50 cycles as input, indicating a small number of early cycles can provide useful indication of final cycle life. These results indicate that explicit physical conditioning and feature-prototype retrieval improve early cycle-life prediction across heterogeneous battery populations.

Generative models of three dimensional structures are judged almost entirely by how they look, yet a building that renders convincingly can still be far too solid, hollow in the wrong places or scattered with loose blocks, and none of that shows in a picture. We take one of the most common designs in 3D generation, in which a model first sketches a coarse outline of a structure and then fills in the detail, and ask on a corpus of human built Minecraft houses whether that outline actually helps, judging every result against what people build rather than against another model. As trained, it does not: across four independent runs the two stage model produces houses more than four times as dense as real ones. When the same detail model is handed outlines taken from real houses instead of its own, the excess largely disappears, which places the fault in the learned outline and not in the idea of conditioning on one. The cause turns out to be ordinary. A loss weighting that helped the detailed stage learn where solid blocks belong was carried over to the outline stage, where it quietly inflated the model’s belief that any given cell is solid, and a single subtraction at sampling time, with no retraining, brings the outlines back to realistic scale. The same bias reached the detailed stage as well, but there the search over sampling temperatures happened to absorb it, and at the coarse stage it could not, which is how one shared setting came to fail in one place and pass unnoticed in the other. Two of our own measures turned out to be tracking size rather than quality, and once they are corrected, density is the one failure left standing. The broader lesson is that every stage of a cascaded generator has to be checked against its own target, because tuning the sampler can hide a miscalibrated stage without ever repairing it.

TL;DR: Every stage of a cascaded generator must be checked against its own target, because sampler tuning can hide a miscalibrated stage without repairing it.

Neural solvers for constrained mechanical systems must recover not only the motion but also the algebraic variables that carry the constraint forces. In regular index-3 differential-algebraic equations these variables are invisible to the position and velocity constraints and become observable only through the hidden acceleration-level constraint. We turn this observation into a design principle for neural trial spaces and propose Index-Aware Subspace Neural Networks (IA-SNN), which learn a neural basis, freeze it, determine the output coefficients by nonlinear least squares on the complete hidden-constraint chain, and select among checkpointed solutions with a reference-free off-collocation residual indicator. We prove that the complete chain yields a local residual-to-solution stability estimate, that chains truncated before the acceleration level admit no such estimate uniformly over trial spaces, and that in polynomial spaces the resulting loss of control grows with resolution. On four closed-form index-3 benchmarks, IA-SNN recovers all fields without failure. A complete residual-chain ablation of physics-informed, random-feature and subspace solvers confirms the graded prediction of the theory, and a constraint-drift comparison with classical integrators shows that satisfying the position constraint says little about the constraint forces. The results separate residual observability, representation quality and read-out optimization, and attribute the gains to observability and checkpoint selection rather than to basis learning itself.

The literature on N:M semi-structured sparsity assumes GPUs with dedicated sparse-compute units, which Apple Silicon lacks. We present, to our knowledge, the first 2:4 semi-structured sparse GEMV kernel for LLM decoding on the Apple Silicon GPU, embedded in a fully fused Metal decoder, and show that 2:4 sparsity pays there because decoding is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute. Against a matched-runtime dense engine, the kernel delivers a 1.42× sparsity-attributable decode speedup on Qwen2.5-1.5B, converting 98.2% of the byte reduction into throughput with sparse and dense paths both sustaining about 67 GB/s; end to end this is 1.93× on short generation and 2.65× at long context (2.88× decode-only) over PyTorch's MPS backend on an 8 GB M2, with prefill at 0.96× (parity with an optional dense prefill mirror on a 16 GB machine), and the same bandwidth model predicts throughput on an M4. To recover quality we keep Wanda's mask and reconstruct block-wise with a calibration set scaled at constant epochs, which reaches a selection-policy-independent optimum (a 1.22× WikiText-2 perplexity ratio at 2048-token context with 32% of parameters removed), and for true 50% all-linear 2:4 we train low-rank adapters jointly with the surviving weights inside the same block objective and execute them in the engine, taking the ratio from 3.01× (one-shot) and 1.91× (reconstruction alone) to 1.52×. The entire pipeline, including adapter training and paired statistical evaluation, runs on the fanless 8 GB laptop. We also report a silent MPS correctness failure above 1024-token contexts and the reference-backend validation rule that catches it.

TL;DR: A 2:4 Semi-Structured Sparse GEMV Kernel for LLM Decoding on Apple Silicon: Sparsity-Attributable Speedups and Laptop-Scale Reconstruction

A user choosing between two models that can answer the same query would prefer
the cheaper model, but only if its decision quality can be trusted relative to an
expensive reference. We generalize this setting to a library of cheap models with
different costs and decision quality, and study how to route among them without
querying the reference for every input. Through the lens of decision stability, we
introduce Decision-Certified Model Routing (DCMR), a stopping rule that accepts
a cheap model when a calibrated bound on its excess decision cost relative to the
expensive reference falls within a given tolerance. The online bound uses only the
selected model’s output; for affine predict-then-optimize tasks, its paired offline
distortion target is computable with a single linear-optimization call. We show that
the certification guarantee is independent of the routing rule. A single maximum
normalized split-conformal score calibrates the model library simultaneously. As
a result, any adaptive routing strategy inherits the same finite-sample marginal
guarantee without requiring model-specific error splitting. Because marginal
validity does not ensure that a selected model is reliable on the particular inputs for
which it is routed, we further audit a frozen policy family on an independent split.
Simultaneous exact binomial bounds certify its conditional failure rate and identify
the least-cost policy satisfying the target guarantee.

TL;DR: We introduce decision-certified model routing (DCMR) for sequential acquisition from a frozen, nonnested predictor library.
